newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Yorks Water factors in windfall tax.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Yorks Water factors in windfall tax.

text.p: British water and sewerage company Yorkshire Water Plc said on Friday it had taken into account a one-off tax proposed by the government in aiming at 6-8 percent real growth annually in cash spent on its dividend, but declined to give details of the figure.
"We have made an assumption for a windfall tax," finance director Brian Wilson told journalists in a conference telephone call, but he declined to give a figure.

Yorkshire, which earlier reported a rise in year pretax profits to 215.8 million stg from 162.2 million and paid out a total dividend of 18.5 pence, up 19 percent on an adjusted basis, could be one of the privatised utilities which the new Labour government has targeted for a one-off "windfall" tax.
Yorkshire chairman Brandon Gough said the company took it for granted there was going to be a windfall tax.
"The issue is on what basis will it be levied as much as how much it will be," he added.

"If the government mean what it says, that it will be focused on clearly defined excess profits, then we would not view it as penalising us because we don't think that our profits are excess," Gough said.
He added that the company had made representations to the Treasury as requested by paymaster general Geoffrey Robinson by the end of May.
Wilson said the company welcomed the government's 10-point plan aimed at tackling the country's worst drought for 200 years, which includes proposals for mandatory leakage targets.
"We welcome the government's commitment, involvement with the industry," he said, adding that Yorkshire already had many conservation measures in place.
Gough said leakage rates were currently running at 26 percent of supplies from the company's pipes and chief executive Kevin Bond said the aim was to reduce that by around one percent this year.
"That'll take us to our 1998 target that we already have," Bond said, adding that Yorkshire was working with industry regulator Ofwat to define a target for 2002-2003.
At the same time, Yorkshire is working to calculate an economic target for leakage -- a level optimising spend with benefit.

Gough said reservoirs in the area were currently at 94 percent of capacity compared with around 60 percent at the same time in 1996 and the company said it should not have to impose restrictions this year, even if conditions were as bad as in 1995.
That year, a severe drought in the traditionally wet area of Yorkshire nearly forced the company to cut essential supplies and it had to tanker in water from outside the region.
Gough said that Yorkshire's achieved progress in improving supplies was "pretty crucial, not just to customer confidence but also investor confidence." -- London Newsroom +44171 542 7717
